The Etiology of Influenza *
A contribution to a discussion on "Influenza" delivered at a meeting of the Royal Medico-Chirurgical Society of Glasgow on 15th November, 1929.

body.preformat: 64 Col. Glen Liston?Th4 Etiology of Influenza. THE BTLOLOGY OF INFLUENZA.* By W. GLEN LISTON, C.I.E., M.D., D.P.H., Lieutenant-Colonel, I.M.S. (retired), Pathologist to the Royal College of Physicians, Edinburgh. Influenza has been a well-recognized disease for centuries. It occurs in widespread epidemics, and attacks large numbers of persons suddenly and almost simultaneously. Prostration and pneumonic complications are features of the disease. The clinical picture in individual cases cannot be drawn so clearly. While a diagnosis of influenza can be made, perhaps with ease, when an epidemic prevails, it is quite otherwise during the inter-epidemic period. The features of the disease are stamped on its epidemic prevalence, not on isolated cases. Therefore, in considering the etiology of influenza, we are confronted with this difficulty at the outset, that the diagnosis of the disease, except in particular circumstances, is uncertain and indefinite. Influenza is without doubt a specific disease like cholera, typhoid, or smallpox, and this presupposes a specific cause. Among the older physicians the view was held that the contagium vivum of influenza was of the nature of a miasma. The disease did not appear to them to be spread by direct contact with the sick; it was not a communicable or a con- tagious disease. They were impressed by the fact that the disease could break out on ships which had no communication with the land for some time; especially if the ship passed on the sea in the neighbourhood of infected countries. Hirsch, for example, quotes the case of an English ship of war cruising on the coast of Cuba in 1857, and holding no communication with the shore, in which the greater part of the crew fell ill of influenza; it was afterwards ascertained that the disease had been prevalent during the same time at Havana, in * A contribution to a discussion on " Influenza " delivered at a meeting of the Eoyal Medico-Chirurgical Society of Glasgow on 15th November, 1929. Col. Glen Ltston?The Etiology of Influenza. 65 Trinidad, and in other West Indian islands. A number of other similar instances are recorded by the same author. The physicians in bygone times were also struck by the speed at which the disease spreads. The epidemic, they said, " affects a whole region in the space of a week, nay a whole continent as large as North America, together with the West Indies, in the course of a few weeks, while the inhabitants could not in so short a time have any communication or inter- course across such a vast extent of country." Hirsch adds significantly " that the disease has not spread more quickly in our times, with their multiplied and perfected ways and means of communication, than in former decades or centuries." Then, again, they were impressed by certain other features of the disease which were not in accord with their experience of an ordinary contagious or infectious disease. For example, the sudden attack of the people en masse and the equally sudden and complete extinction of the disease after a brief existence. They noticed also that the disease might be restricted to one place while the whole country around remained free. They thought that domestic animals participated in the disease, especially horses, and, to a less extent, dogs and cats. Our modern views of the epidemiology of influenza are at complete variance with the views held by the physicians of past centuries. We believe that the disease is highly contagious. Could a more striking example of this fact be instanced than that given by Dr. Ferguson? And yet, while the contagious nature of the disease can hardly be disputed, it is remarkable to note how difficult it is to communicate the disease experi- mentally even to men. So far as I know, nobody now adheres to the view that our domestic animals suffer from influenza; certainly the decrease in the number of horses on our streets owing to the increased use of motor cars has not diminished the intensity or virulence of the disease. I hold in my hand a publication of the United States Public Health Service, Bulletin No. 123, published in February, 1921, which describes attempts to communicate influenza to rather more than 160 volunteers. These experi- ments were carried out by Kosenau, McCoy and others. They attempted to infect volunteers in a variety of ways. In some 66 Col. Glen Ltston?The Etiology of Influenza. experiments cultures of certain organisms were used which were thought to be possible causes of the disease. In other experiments the washings from the nose and throat of infected persons were employed to incite the disease in the healthy. These washings were sometimes filtered, at other times they were used unfiltered, and they were applied by spraying or by gargling. Experiments were also made with material transferred on swabs from the throats of the acutely sick to the throats of the volunteers. Infection by contact was also thoroughly exploited, as the following experiment shows :? Ten volunteers were used; they were taken to the ward of a hospital in which thirty cases of influenza were being treated, and they were exposed to infection in the following way :? Each volunteer took up a position close to the bedside of a selected patient and conversed with him for two or three minutes. Then the patient was directed to breathe five times and then cough five times directly into the face of the volunteer. After this was done the volunteer proceeded to the bedside of a second patient. In this manner each of the volunteers was exposed in succession to each of ten patients, selected because all were in the acute stage of the disease; they had developed symptoms only ten to seventy-two hours previously. Each volunteer was thus exposed to each patient for from three to five minutes. The total exposure of each volunteer, therefore, was between thirty and fifty minutes. Not one of the volunteers developed any indication of illness following this exposure. This is but one of many experiments; I have selected it to give you some idea of the care and thoroughness with which the tests were made. The authors are careful to say that their experiments do not warrant any positive conclusion. They are surprised, nevertheless, at the negative character of their results, for they regard the disease as very contagious, and in support of this view they state that the incident rate in the actual epidemic was usually 20 per cent, often 30 per cent, or more of the population. You must read the experiments in detail to understand their significance. Only three of the 160 volunteers purposely exposed to infection developed symptoms which the experi- menters recognized as influenza. It is noteworthy, however, Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza. 67 that there were as many as thirteen other persons of the 160 subjected to infection who suffered from sore throat or tonsil- litis, and in this connexion the difficulty in diagnosing the disease must be kept in mind. Similar experiments have been carried out by Lister in South Africa, and by other persons in other parts of the world, with like findings. The conclusion must be drawn that it is difficult to convey the disease experimentally from the sick to the healthy and that the exact circumstances in which infection becomes possible are not yet known or understood. The pandemic of influenza of the years 1889-1892 was the first to occur in what may be regarded as the beginning of the bacteriological era. Many workers during these years studied the bacteriology of the disease; some offered one bacterium, others another, as its cause; many were confused by the number and variety of the micro-organisms which might be found invading the body of the sick. In 1892 Pfeiffer announced that the disease, in his opinion, was due to a minute Gram-negative bacillus which grows in culture media only in the presence of blood or some derivative thereof. He called this organism Bacillus influenzce. Pfeiffer's bacillus was almost universally accepted by bacteriologists for a time as the true cause of influenza, but the widespread pandemic of 1918-1919 caused some of them to abandon this view. These bacteriologists either failed to isolate Pfeiffer's bacillus in many cases of undoubted influenza or they found a very similar, if not identical, bacillus in persons suffering from other diseases or even in healthy persons. The mysterious infectivity of the 1918-1919 pandemic suggested to some a mysterious or at least an unusual cause for the disease. Kruse's suggestion that the disease might be caused by an ultra-microscopic or filtrable virus obtained many adherents. He believed that he had shown that a common cold was caused by a filter passing virus. The throats of infected persons were therefore washed with saline, the washings were collected and filtered and the cause of the disease looked for in the filtrate either by injecting men or animals with the material or by making cultures from it after the manner adopted by Noguchi for cultivating filter passing organisms. 68 Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza. Working 011 these lines, the discovery of the cause of the disease has been claimed by Nicol and Labailley, by Gibson and his co-workers, and by Rose Bradford and others. Subsequent investigation and criticism by other workers of their work has not substantiated their claims, and Rose Bradford has had the courage to acknowledge his error in the interpretation of his experiments. The work of Olitsky and Gates, however, on the same lines, is quite in another category. Their elaborate and extensive experiments have been confirmed, at least in part, by a few other workers. They state that the organism which they claim to be the cause of the disease is found in the nose and throat of an infected person only in the early stages of the disease, i.e., within thirty-six hours of the onset of symptoms. Bacterium pneumosintes, as they call their organism, cannot be recovered from persons in the later stages of the disease. The organism is able to pass through the pores of a Berkefeld V or N filter, and it is strictly anaerobic in its growth. In the early stages of their investigation, it was cultivated by Noguchi's method and was then found to be a very minute bacillus; later they cultivated their organism on blood agar. It produces, they claim, very characteristic colonies on this medium, readily distinguishable from the colonies produced by other filter passing micro-organisms found in normal persons. Cultivated in this way it becomes a relatively large bacillus compared with that developed on Noguchi's medium?not much smaller, in fact, than Pfeiffer's bacillus. Like that organism it is also Gram-negative. Olitsky and Gates claim that they have obtained definite serological reactions, agglutination, precipitation and compli- ment fixation, in the blood of persons who have recovered from influenza. But, so far as I can gather, they hold the view that their organism is mainly important in bringing about such changes in the tissues as allow the invasion of the body by other organisms?such as Pfeiffer's bacillus, streptococci, staphylococci and pneumococci. They maintain that these latter organisms, which are found in the blood and tissues of persons suffering from influenza, are normal saprophytes of the respiratory tract, and that they only become pathogenic, i.e., capable of producing definite lesions, when bacterium pneumosintes has damaged the tissues and thus allowed them Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza. 69 to overcome the normal defensive mechanism of the body which keeps them at bay and permits them normally to exist as saprophytes. It seems to me that Olitsky and Gates have made out a strong case in favour of their view that bacterium pnenmosintes is the primary or exciting cause of influenza, and it is unfortunate, therefore, that those who have attempted, without success, to repeat their experiments have almost always departed in some small, though possibly important, detail from the technique laid down by them. The best work which has been done in this connexion is that by Wilson, who, however, used a Chamber- lain filter in place of a Y or N Berkefeld candle. There are many bacteriologists, however, who are not pre- pared to accept the somewhat novel views held by Olitsky and Gates on the pathology of influenza. They still seek some other cause for the disease, or they may cling to Pfeiffer's bacillus as satisfying their needs. Leaving the cause of influenza still an open question, let me for a few minutes give you some of my personal experiences connected with the study of this disease. Like many bacterio- logists, I made my first acquaintance with influenza during the pandemic of 1918-1919. I was then in charge of a large Bacteriological Laboratory at Parel, Bombay, and was consult- ing pathologist to the hospitals in that city. I had abundant opportunity, in conjunction with my colleagues in the laboratory, to study the disease, especially in a large hospital for military followers situated near the laboratory. We found, as many others had found, that it was possible to recover a variety of organisms from the blood and tissues of infected persons. Among these Pfeiffer's bacillus was occasionally met with, but we had great difficulty in growing the organisms, especially in subcultures, even on blood agar. This was a matter of some importance for us, for we were asked to prepare for the use of the Army large quantities of influenza vaccine in accord with the formula prescribed by the Army Council. Although this vaccine contained only a very small proportion of influenza bacilli we experienced great difficulty in obtaining a sufficient quantity for our needs. I accordingly set all the staff of the laboratory to work to find some better way to grow the influenza bacillus. After a number of trials 70 Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Ivfiuevza. two types of media were discovered which yielded good growths. One medium devised by my colleague, Dr. Soparker, was particularly successful. It is prepared by adding to one volume of blood drawn from a vein aseptically four volumes of 05 per cent sodium citrate in normal saline (0 85 per cent) solution. This diluted blood is heated for half an hour at a temperature between 64? and 68? C. A brown coagulum or precipitate is formed which is separated by filtration through paper in an aseptic manner, the clear port-wine coloured filtrate is then passed through a Seitz's bacterial filter and is stored in quantities of about *20 c.c. in sterile test tubes. Ten per cent of this blood extract is added to culture media for use in the cultivation of the influenza bacillus. The use of this medium enabled us to find influenza bacilli with ease in a number of cases of the disease, but by this time the epidemic was almost over in Bombay and our attention was concentrated on the - preparation of vaccine. Our failure to find the influenza bacillus in many of our earlier cases was due, without doubt, to the lack of a suitable medium for its cultivation. I had not another opportunity to study influenza till I was invited, in 1926, by Drs. McNeil, Macgregor, and Alexander to co-operate with them in the study of broncho-pneumonia in children, and to investigate the bacteriological cause of this very fatal malady. I went to the first "post-mortem examination armed with the ordinary culture media used in laboratories; I did not expect to be confronted with a study of influenza, but the naked-eye post-mortem appearances reminded me of that type of broncho-pneumonia which I had seen associated with influenza in India, and I regretted that I had not brought with me at this first postmortem examination the special medium referred to above for cultivating the influenza bacillus. In subsequent examinations this deficiency was remedied, and I have published in the Archives of Diseases of Childhood (vol. iv, October, 1929) my bacteriological findings in 40 cases of fatal broncho-pneumonia in children. I should like to refer very briefly to these findings, and show you some photographs of some of my cultures. I may state that Pfeiffer's bacillus was found in a very large percentage of the cases examined; but this statement by itself has little value, other facts must be taken into consideration Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza, 71 in appraising the relation of that bacillus to the lesions produced in the disease. First, I would like to show you that in early and acute cases an almost pure culture of Pfeiffer's bacillus may be obtained from the lung if fluid is withdrawn by puncture through the pleura. In these cases where a pure culture is obtained by lung puncture, cultures from the sputum show many colonies of Pfeiffer's bacillus, but other organisms are present also, sometimes in considerable numbers. In cases which have advanced a stage further the culture plates made from a lung puncture, while still showing a marked preponderance of influenza colonies, also show colonies of other organisms as well, and in cultures from the sputum of the same cases these colonies of secondary invading organisms, staphylococci, streptococci, pneumococci, and others, increase markedly in proportion to the influenza colonies. In still later cases, where the lung tissue has begun to break down and abscesses are beginning to develop, it may be difficult to beginning to develop, it may be difficult to demonstrate colonies made by lung puncture. Pfeiffer's organism in these cases in this position has been replaced by staphylococci, streptococci, and a host of other organisms. In very advanced cases where the lungs have become gangrenous, vast numbers of bacteria of all kinds are now to be found. In cultures made from fluid obtained by lung puncture no colonies of Pfeiffer's bacilli may be demonstrated, but this organism may be recovered on plates made from fluid drawn from the enlarged lymphatic glands at the root of the lungs. By way of recapitulation I wish to impress upon you that Pfeiffer's bacillus was isolated in almost pure culture in many of these cases of broncho-pneumonia when the cultures were made from material obtained at the advancing edge of the lesions in the lungs. Behind this advancing margin, where damage had been done by Pfeiffer's bacillus, other organisms were found. These secondary invading organisms, multiplying greatly, in turn cause further damage and gradually replace Pfeiffer's bacillus. Thus, in cases where abscesses had formed or the lung had become gangrenous it was difficult or impossible to find any of the organisms which were the primary cause of the trouble in these situations, 72 Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza. While speaking of the difficulty of isolating Pfeiffer's bacillus in the presence of large numbers of secondary invading organisms I should like to direct your attention to Fleming's work on the use of penicillin published in a paper which appeared in vol. x of the British Journal of Experimental Pathology. Fleming has given the name " penicillin " to the active principle contained in sterile filtrate of a culture of Penicillium rubrum in broth which has been grown at room temperature for about seven days. This filtrate has the property of dissolving cultures or suspensions of certain strains of staphylococcus, pneumococcus, or streptococcus. When it is added in a suitable quantity to a medium which is in other respects favourable for the growth of Pfeiffer's bacillus the penicillin inhibits the growth of certain strains of staphy- lococcus, pneumococcus, and streptococcus, while it has no effect on Pfeiffer's bacillus, which in these circumstances grows freely. The photographs which I now show you demonstrate that the use of penicillin greatly facilitates the isolation of Pfeiffer's bacillus and allied hsemophyllic organisms when it is added to Soparker's medium. Now, while Pfeiffer's bacillus multiplies locally in the invaded tissues it seldom gains an entrance to the blood-stream, although occasionally it is found in this situation either in pure culture or more commonly with other organisms such as strains of streptococcus and pneumococcus. These latter organisms effect an entrance to the body of their host through damage wrought by Pfeiffer's bacillus. They are found in situations which are normally selected by each strain. For example, certain strains of streptococcus multiply in the blood, in a serous or a synovial cavity, while the pleural cavity is the site of election for the pneumococcus although sometimes it may be found in the blood or cerebro-spinal fluid. In the forty cases of fatal broncho-pneumonia in children which I have studied Pfeiffer's bacillus was present in pure culture in the blood of the heart in one case only. It was present, however, in that situation with other organisms in five other cases, twice with a strain of streptococcus, once with a coliform organism and a staphylococcus, and once with a coliform organism and a pneumococcus. On another occasion Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza. 73 Pfeiffer's bacillus was isolated from the blood together with two distinct strains of pneumococcus. It was also found in pure culture in the cerebro-spinal fluid in one of the cases and in recent pleural adhesions in another. It was present in the pus in a pleural cavity in two other cases; in one of these with a pneumococcus, and in the other with both a pneumococcus and a streptococcus. There was some evidence to show that Pfeiffer's bacillus probably gained an entrance to the blood by way of the lymphatic system, for the lymphatic glands at the hilum of the lungs were greatly enlarged in almost all the cases. A streptococcus was isolated from the heart in pure culture in six of the cases and in two more together with Pfeiffer's bacillus. This organism was often found in large numbers in pus from abscesses in the lungs, and it was present in the pleura and peritoneum in other cases. A pneumococcus was found in the heart blood in pure culture in one case only, while in two other cases it was present there together with Pfeiffer's bacillus. In one of these latter cases two distinct strains of pneumococcus were present in the blood at the same time. Perhaps the most striking case of infection by more than one organism was that one in which a pure culture of a streptococcus was isolated from the peritoneum, a pure culture of a pneumococcus obtained from a pleural cavity, while another culture showed that Pfeiffer's bacillus was abundantly present in the lung just beneath the surface of the pleura. On the whole, this study showed that Pfeiffer's bacillus played an important role in the causation of broncho-pneumonia. Now, I believe that these cases of broncho-pneumonia were in reality cases of influenza. My reasons for holding this view may be summarized as follows :?First, broncho-pneumonia is a well-recognized complication of influenza; secondly, both the bacteriological findings and the histological features of sections of the lungs exactly tally with those of other workers who have studied the broncho-pneumonia associated with influenza in adults; thirdly, the cases occurred in definite groups suggesting epidemic conditions. On this chart the shaded columns represent the number of cases of broncho-pneumonia as they came for post-mortem No. 2. E Vol CXIII. 74 Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza. examination each month during the four years covered by the inquiry. A single case is represented on this chart as a shaded square; when two squares are placed over one another a column is formed, so that the height of the shaded columns is a measure of the number of cases which were examined in each particular month. Now, I wish to point out that by the time we had entered on the fourth year of our inquiry I had become so persuaded of the relationship between epidemic influenza and cases of fatal broncho-pneumonia in children that I was able to forecast the occurrence of more cases early in the year 1929, for at that time an epidemic of influenza prevailed. Eight cases were actually examined in February of that year. About this time I was engaged in testing the efficiency of a vaccine against influenza, and had occasion to inoculate a number of nurses in the Royal Infirmary in Edinburgh. On one of my visits to the Matron's Office I noticed a chart on the wall which had been maintained for some years. It showed each day the number of nurses who were off duty on account of sickness. The chart demonstrated, as was to be expected when an epidemic of influenza prevailed, that the number of nurses off duty each day had rapidly increased. Through the kindness of the Matron I was permitted to examine this chart more carefully. I observed that, in addition to the elevation of the curve which was caused by the then Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza. 75 prevailing epidemic of influenza, there were other well-marked elevations present on the chart, which, as I have said, covered a period of years. These elevations of the curve represented other epidemics, some of which were possibly influenza. In order to demonstrate clearly when these epidemics occurred, I added up the number of nurses who were sick each day during a period of four years and struck a mean number of " daily sick " for the whole period. This gave me the figure 15. I next calculated the average daily sick for each month through- out the period, and found, of course, that these numbers in some months exceeded the mean, in other months they fell below the mean. This variation I expressed as a percentage above and below the mean, and I have shown it on the chart as a dark line. It will be observed that there were four periods during the four years when the number of sick rose well above the mean. The most marked of these epidemics was that which attained its highest point in February, 1929. This was a well-recognized epidemic of influenza. Lesser epidemics occurred in January, 1928, in March, 1927, and in March and April, 1926. You will observe that there is a fairly close correlation between the epidemics among the nurses and the cases of broncho-pneumonia in children which came to post- mortem examination. The agreement is not good, however, in that epidemic which occurred among the nurses in January, 1928. In this connexion I must explain that post-mortem examinations were not made during the Christmas and New-Year holidays, so that this may account for the absence of agreement at this time. When due allowance is made for the small number of cases of broncho-pneumonia which were examined post-mortem the correlation between these examina- tions and epidemics among the nurses is, to say the least, striking. In closing my remarks I should like to make a brief reference again to the difficulty of diagnosing influenza in the absence of epidemic conditions. The development of the epidemic among the nurses in 1929 presented a striking case. You will observe from the chart that the amount of sickness among the nurses began to increase rapidly in December; it attained epidemic proportions in January, and reached the highest point in February. The number of nurses diagnosed as suffering 76 Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza. from tonsillitis increased with the increase in the number of the sick; there was then no thought of influenza as a cause of the sickness. In January the increase in the number of sick nurses was now well marked, but still only one or two cases of influenza were recognized among them, while in February, the existence of the epidemic being now well known, the bulk of the sickness was diagnosed as influenza. I am at present engaged in an inquiry which aims at finding by a bacteriological examination the beginning of an epidemic of influenza. This involves the examination of the throat of every nurse when she is admitted to hospital. I have already examined the throats of some eighty nurses during an inter- epidemic period. Some light has been shed on the existence of hnemophyllic bacilli which resemble Pfeiffer's bacillus. I can generally differentiate these influenza-like organisms from true influenza bacilli by certain sugar fermentation reactions. I have found that by adding the blood extract, the preparation of which I have already described to you, in a strength of 10 per cent to a solution of 1 per cent Witte's peptone in normal (0-85 per cent) saline, I can obtain a good medium for the cultivation of the hgemophyllic organisms. This stock solution must be accurately titrated so as to have a pH of 7-5, and to 100 c.c. of it 1-5 c.c. of a 04 per cent solution of phenol red is added. To separate volumes of this fluid 1 per cent of the following sugars is added, viz., sucrose, lactose, maltose, fructose, galactose, xylose and glucose. The fluid prepared in this way should not be sterilized by heat, but filtered through a Seitz's bacterial filter and stored in tubes for use. I find that Pfeiffer's bacillus, i.e., Bacillus influenzae, in this medium fails to ferment the disaccharides succrose, lactose, and maltose, while the largest number of the strains I have tested ferment all the monosaccharides mentioned. There are, however, two subsidiary groups which in other respects resemble the large group just mentioned, except that in one the organisms fail to ferment galactose and in the other they fail to ferment xylose. There is yet another group of hsemophyllic Gram-negative bacilli the members of which very closely resemble the true influenza bacillus. The two strains belonging to this group Col. Glen Liston?The Etiology of Influenza. 77 which I have met with were isolated from chronic lesions in the nose; they resemble the true influenza strains in all respects except that thev can ferment maltose. There is still another group of hsemophyllic Gram-negative bacilli, the members of which are frequently encountered in the throats of normal and sick persons. These fail to ferment any of the sugars I have mentioned, except perhaps one or two of them to a very slight extent. Some of these strains ferment succrose. In conclusion, I believe that those bacteriologists who have abandoned the view that Pfeiffer's bacillus is the cause of influenza have done so because they have failed to use a suitable culture medium for the isolation of the bacillus, or they have mistaken other organisms which they have found in normal persons for the true influenza bacillus. Pfeiffer's influenza bacillus, in my opinion, is not a normal saprophyte of the air passages; there are some reasons for believing that it is the cause of influenza.
